title: Gemini Daily Brief could soon be actually useful all day long
summary: You might soon be able to refresh your Daily Brief on demand.
body: Credit: Stephen Radochia / Android Authority TL;DR Gemini Daily Brief currently generates a static morning recap that cannot be manually updated as your day or schedule changes. Code found in Google app v17.58.13 indicates Google is working on a new “Refresh daily brief” option to regenerate Daily Brief content on demand. The feature is currently in development and isn’t fully functional yet, but it could potentially pull fresh context from your calendar, emails, and tasks. Google appears to be gearing up to fix one of the biggest annoyances with the Gemini Daily Brief. Google has been actively expanding access to the feature, including making the Gemini Daily Brief available to free users and experimenting with quick audio briefing shortcuts . However, Daily Brief remains curiously rigid once it compiles your morning summary. That could soon change, as Google appears to be testing a dedicated manual refresh trigger to regenerate your briefing on demand. You’re reading an Authority Insights story. title: I don’t care about 7 years of Android updates, and you shouldn’t either
summary: Don't let the marketing fool you.
body: Credit: Pankil Shah / Android Authority Every Android phone manufacturer, be it Google, Samsung, or any other, loves to flex its seven-year OS update promise as the ultimate way to “future-proof” your purchase. But I don’t think it plays out the same way in reality. Sure, an Android phone can easily last six or seven years — that part isn’t in question. The real problem is that these longer updates mean nothing without new features, and even less if they just slow the phone down. That’s the part that companies obviously don’t talk about, but it’s what I want to discuss right now.

title: A Galaxy S25 FE user blamed One UI for battery drain, turns out it was something entirely different
summary: A user's Galaxy S25 FE started overheating and experiencing severe drain recently. The culprit was unexpected.
body: Credit: C. Scott Brown / Android Authority TL;DR A Galaxy S25 FE user recently thought a recent One UI update was causing their phone to overheat. Digging deeper revealed a WhatsApp background service was malfunctioning. WhatsApp wasn’t at fault either, as the conflict arose from two different instances of Google Play Services. One of them was due to an unofficial spoofer — MicroG — used to run to modded YouTube apps, such as ReVanced. It’s often easy to blame the latest software updates for poor device performance, but that might not always be the case.
